MELATONIN

James Meschino DC, MS, ROHP

Melatonin is a molecule that has been found in every animal and plant studied to date, from
human beings to the most primitive one-celled algae that evolved more than three billion years
ago.  In each organism, the molecular structure of melatonin is identical.  This sameness is a rare
occurrence in nature. In all the life forms studied, melatonin has been produced in the same
circadian (daily secretion pattern) rhythm, with higher levels produced at night than during the
daytime.
In humans, melatonin is produced and secreted by the pineal gland in the brain.  It is synthesized
from the brain chemical (neurotransmitter) serotonin, which itself is synthesized from 5-
hydroxytryptophan, which is originally derived from the amino acid tryptophan, found in many
foods. In the human body melatonin acts as a hormone, neurotransmitter (brain chemical),
antioxidant and immune system stimulator. This tremendous versatility accounts for the many
profound effects that melatonin exerts on our health status.
As a neurotransmitter (brain chemical) melatonin is best known for its ability to induce sleep in
persons with insomnia and to remedy problems with interrupted sleep, as well as its ability to
elevate mood.  Humans produce five to ten times more melatonin at night than during the day, a
circadian rhythm found in animals as well.  Peak amounts occur around two or three o'clock in
the morning. The darker the room, the more melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland at night.
After puberty the body's production of melatonin has been shown to decline.  By age 40 humans
often produce approximately 60 percent less melatonin than a 10 year old and by age 70 or 80
melatonin levels may be undetectable.  The use of certain drugs, such as aspirin, ibuprofen, and

beta-blockers (used to control high blood pressure) also contributes to a decline in melatonin
levels.
With respect to its antioxidant properties, melatonin is unique in that it is both a water-soluble
antioxidant and a fat-soluble antioxidant.  This means that it can quench and intercept dangerous
free radicals in every area of the body and in every part of every cell in the body. Not even
vitamin C or vitamin E has this range of antioxidant capability. Some studies suggest that as an
antioxidant melatonin is twice as effective as Vitamin E, five times as efficient as glutathione,
and five hundred times more effective than the synthetic DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide).  However,
melatonin is produced in picograms (a trillionth of a gram – the smallest amount of any
hormone), whereas Vitamin E, and other antioxidants, are present in the body at much higher
concentrations.
The decline in melatonin synthesis and secretion by the pineal gland is considered to be a very
significant factor that contributes to less restful sleep, accelerated aging and increased risk of
certain cancers, dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and a weakening of our immune system as we
age. Many anti-aging experts recommend taking a melatonin supplement by age 50, as studies
suggest that providing more youthful levels of melatonin to your brain and body can help combat
aging, boost immune system function, reduce cancer and heart disease risk and produce better
quality sleep and mood enhancement.
Melatonin for a Good Night's Sleep
We sleep roughly 16 hours as infants, 8 hours in adolescence, 7 hours as adults, and less than 6
hours in our geriatric years.  No one seems to be exactly sure how melatonin induces better
quality, restful sleep, but the reduced output of melatonin as we age is strongly associated with
decreased sleep duration, a greater tendency towards interrupted sleep, and a lesser ability to
achieve deeper levels of sleep. Delta sleep, the deepest most restorative stage of sleep is longer in

childhood, decreases at puberty, and progressively declines after age 30. The elderly spend less
time in this restorative stage and therefore, are likely to feel tired during the day. This accounts
for the fact that as we get older we often feel the need to rest more, but rarely feel completely
rested, rejuvenated, and completely re-energized after a night's sleep, as we did when we were
children.

Melatonin is made in the pineal gland from serotonin, which is a mood enhancing, appetite
suppressing, brain chemical (neurotransmitter). Daylight stimulates the production of serotonin
in our brain. That is one of the reason we feel so much better on a bright, sunny day, as the more
sunlight that enters the pupil of the eye, the greater is the synthesis of serotonin in our brain.
Darkness allows serotonin to be converted into melatonin in the pineal gland, and the darker the
room the more melatonin we secrete through the night. Starting in the evening, and through out
the night, the pineal gland releases melatonin, reaching peak levels between 2 and 4 am. In the
morning, exposure to light shuts off melatonin production.

An interesting study reported in the British Medical Journal in 1994 showed that the quality of
sleep in elderly individuals is proportional to the amount of melatonin secreted by their pineal
gland. Evidence suggests that cells within the pineal gland decrease in number as we age,
making them less efficient in producing melatonin, which in part, accounts for the decline in
melatonin secretions as we get older. Studies show that melatonin supplementation taken one
hour prior to bedtime helps individuals proceed more quickly into stage 2 sleep (early stage of
sleep) and remain longer in the deeper levels of sleep (stage 3, 4, and REM sleep-dream time
sleep) than occurs without melatonin supplementation.

One of the ways that melatonin supplementation can strengthen our immune system is by helping
us attain deeper levels of sleep, as it is known that the immune system is most active during stage
3 and stage 4 sleep (delta sleep). However, many immune cells are also directly influenced by
melatonin, which has been shown to enhance many parameters of immune function.

Studies conducted on humans have shown that melatonin is an effective sleep aid, allowing older
subjects to experience the deeper, rejuvenating, immune-enhancing form of sleep we enjoyed in
our youth. As a sleep aid, melatonin has been shown to be safer than other sleeping pills, which
come with a host of side effects and toxicity problems. Melatonin toxicity studies demonstrate
that it is not only extremely non-toxic and safe, but it also provides many other health-
promoting, anti-aging benefits to the body beyond improving our sleep quality. Taken at the right
dosage, one hour before bedtime, melatonin does not produce morning drowsiness, and helps to
elevate mood and feeling of well being though out the day, which is probably due to its chemical
resemblance to serotonin – the mood elevating brain chemical. Anti-aging experts suggest that
we begin using melatonin supplementation between age 40 and 50, as a means to improve sleep
quality, support immune function, and to help reduce our risk of cancer, dementia, Alzheimer's
disease and possibly heart disease.
Melatonin May Prevent Breast and Prostate Cancer
The decline in melatonin secretion as we age may allow breast cancer and prostate cancer to
develop more easily, which may partially account for the increased incidence in these cancers as
we get older. Studies demonstrate that melatonin has an anti-estrogen effect on reproductive
tissues, which has been shown to tone down the over stimulation effect of estrogen on breast

cells, an effect that is associated with decreased risk of breast cancer development. Some early
studies demonstrated that women who sleep in darker rooms throughout their lifetime, and who
therefore have higher secretion rates of melatonin through the night, have a lower risk of breast
cancer during their lifetime than do women who sleep in a room that is less dark.

More recently, experimental studies have shown that melatonin can reduce the replication rate of
human breast cancer cells by 50-75%, when these cells were exposed to alternating levels of
melatonin to mimic the body's day and night time melatonin secretion patterns. This was only
true in regards to breast cancer cells that possess estrogen receptors on their surface (estrogen-
receptor-positive breast cells), which indicates that melatonin likely latches on to estrogen
receptors, as does the hormone estrogen, but rather than stimulate these cells to divide rapidly, it
inhibits or slows their cell division rate. This is similar to the action of the drug Tamoxifen,
which is used to prevent the recurrence of breast cancer and its metastases, in women that have
estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer. In fact, experimental studies have shown that melatonin
can enhance the ability of Tamoxifen to inhibit the replication of breast cancer cells. These
studies prompted Dr. Paolo Lissoni to combine Tamoxifen therapy and melatonin
supplementation (20 mg twice per day) in a trial of breast cancer patients. The study showed that
four out of the fourteen women had a 50% or greater reduction in the size of their tumors. Eight
additional women showed no further progression in tumor size. Only two women failed to
respond to the treatment. These results were better than the typical outcomes associated with
Tamoxifen use alone. Larger studies of this kind are underway presently to better understand the
use of melatonin as a cancer therapy agent.

However, from the standpoint of prevention, the body of evidence suggests that melatonin may
protect against breast cancer in several ways. First, it antagonizes the effects of estrogen on
breast cells, helping to slow down the rate of cell division, which in turn, decreases the chance of
a cancer cell developing. Second, should a cancer cell develop in the breast, melatonin has been
shown to inhibit its ability to divide and spread, giving the body's immune system a better
opportunity to kill it off before it can really take hold and become a life threatening problem.
Thirdly, melatonin enhances the effectiveness of the Natural Killer Cells, an important immune
cell that seeks out developing cancer cells and kills them before they can start to divide and
thrive in the body. Also keep in mind that melatonin is a powerful antioxidant that helps to
prevent free radical damage (and the genetic mutations they cause) to all body tissues and all
cellular components, including the DNA of breast cells. Thus, the lower melatonin levels that are
found in a woman's body after 50 years of age (men and women 51-55 years of age secrete half
as much melatonin at night as is secreted at age 21-25; melatonin secretion is four times lower in
men and women 82-86 years of age than at age 21-25) may reduce a woman's ability to prevent
the development and spread of breast cancer. Thus, many anti-aging experts recommend that
women take 200 mcg (.2 mg) -3,000 mcg (3 mg) of melatonin an hour before bedtime each
night, beginning at age 40-50, to re-acquire the protective levels of melatonin that may help
guard against breast cancer in younger women.

In regards to prostate cancer, studies by R. Philo and A. Berkowitz, published in the Journal of
Urology in 1988, showed that melatonin inhibits the growth and replication of human prostate
cancer cells. More recently, an experimental study by David Blask and another group of
researchers demonstrated similar findings, showing a 50% reduction in prostate cancer cell
growth and replication when these cells were incubated with melatonin. Like breast cancer

patients, males with diagnosed prostate cancer have been shown to have low blood levels of
melatonin. However, we are not sure at this point if the low melatonin levels increased the risk of
prostate and breast cancer development or if these cancers cause a reduction in melatonin levels.

There is one important case study that showed that melatonin supplementation at 6 mg per day
was able to reduce the PSA level from 30 to 4 within six months in a confirmed case of localized
prostate cancer. The PSA (prostate specific antigen blood level) is an indirect marker of the
activity of the tumor. A normal PSA level is 0-4. Thus, it may be advantageous for men with
prostate cancer, who are in the watchful waiting stage of the condition, to take 6-10 mg of
melatonin one hour before bedtime each night. This intervention may help reverse or better
control prostate cancer cell activity, which may help improve outcomes from concurrent or
future medical interventions (drugs, surgery, radiation treatment).

However, in regards to prevention, the body of evidence suggests that melatonin
supplementation by age 40-50 years of age, may be another intervention that can help deter
development of prostate cancer, which remains the most frequently diagnosed cancer in men in
North America.

Dr. Lissoni and colleagues, from the division of oncological radiotherapy at Gerardo Hospital in
Milan, Italy, have been on the forefront of melatonin research as it applies to cancer prevention
and treatment. They have administered melatonin in daily doses of 20 mg per day, in conjunction
with the use of standard drugs and related cancer treatments, in cases of advanced lung, colon,
and metastatic brain cancer. Their preliminary studies have shown that melatonin can improve

outcomes in a significant number of these cases, when added to traditional medical treatment.
Further studies are underway to evaluate the role of melatonin as an adjunct to cancer treatment
for a variety of cancers. In the meantime, its ability to inhibit the growth of human breast and
prostate cancer cells under experimental conditions, along with its other anti-cancer properties,
make melatonin supplementation a strong consideration for men and women over 40 years of
age, to compensate for the age-related decline in melatonin secretion rates that become
significant at this stage in life.

Melatonin Boosts Immune Function

Many studies have shown that melatonin can boost various aspects of immune function and thus,
the decline in melatonin levels as we age may be an significant contributing factor to the parallel
decline in immune function that occurs after age 40 to 50. Receptors for melatonin have been
found in lymphoid organs such as the thymus gland and spleen, and on certain white blood cells.
Some studies suggest that melatonin can help restore thymus gland function and prevent age-
related thymus gland degeneration. Studies on mice demonstrate that melatonin can enhance
immune function even when mice were given cortisol, a drug known to suppress the immune
system. Melatonin supplementation also showed that it could keep the immune system working
at a more optimal level in mice that were subjected to various types of stress. Stress is also
known to suppress immune function, but melatonin administration buffered the immune system
against the effects of stress to a significant degree in these studies.

The work of researchers G.J. Maestroni and A. Contri, and fellow investigators, has provided us
with an important piece of the puzzle as to how melatonin helps to optimize the function of our
immune system. They have shown that the T-Helper Cells of our immune system have receptors
for melatonin. When melatonin attaches to these receptors a cascade of events is set into motion
that significantly boosts our immune function. Once melatonin docks to the receptors on our T-
Helper Cells, they in turn stimulate the release of an important immune system signaling agent
known as interleukin-4 (IL-4), which increases the production and efficiency of Natural Killer
Cells, and stimulates immune cells to more efficiently engulf and destroy various micro-
organisms (viruses, bacteria, yeast fungi etc.). Studies show that taking 2 mg of melatonin at
night can increase the production of Natural Killer Cells by 240% compared to pre-melatonin
supplementation levels. Natural Killer Cells specialize in attacking cancer cells and virus-
infected cells, two extremely important aspects in the prevention of cancer and the infections
disease process, served by our immune system. The release of IL-4 also stimulates the
production of a hormone-like substance (granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor) that
increases the production of white blood cells in our bone marrow. White blood cells are the cells
of the immune system that battle infections and cancer cells in our bloodstream and in all the
tissues and organs of the body.

The importance of T-Helper Cells in coordinating the movements, proliferation and efficiency of
our immune cells (white blood cells) is highlighted by the fact that the primary way in which the
HIV-virus exerts its lethal effects is by infecting our T-Helper cells, suppressing their function
and decreasing their numbers in the body. When T-Helper Cell concentrations fall below a
critical threshold (200 cells per microliter) due to infection with the HIV-virus, this is the point
where AIDS begins, whereby opportunistic infections, general deterioration and increased

susceptibility to malignancy become more prevalent in these cases. In fact, studies by G.
Maestoni and fellow researchers have shown that melatonin supplementation of 20 mg per day
(taken at 7:00 PM), given to fourteen patients with HIV infection or full blown AIDS was able to
raise the T-Helper Cell blood count by 35%, on average. It also raised the concentrations of
Natural Killer Cells by 57%, and raised the levels of one type of lymphocyte by 76%. None of
the patients had any adverse side effects from melatonin supplementation at this dosage. Other
studies by Dr. Maestoni as well as Dr. Lissoni, have shown that the melatonin supplementation
can produce a number of favorable outcomes on the immune system in HIV and AIDS patients,
when administered in conjunction with other standard HIV drugs. These studies provide
definitive evidence that melatonin enhances important aspects of immune function, even in
individuals with compromised immune diseases.

There is reason to believe that daily melatonin supplementation after age 40-50, when our body's
secretion rates of this hormone have reached a critical point of decline, may be highly
advantageous in preventing the deterioration in immune function that commonly accompanies
the normal aging process and makes us more prone to cancer and life-threatening infectious
diseases.
Melatonin May Reduce Risk of Alzheimer's Disease and Age-Related Cognitive
Impairment

Melatonin is not only made by a gland in the brain (pineal gland), but may be the brain's most
powerful antioxidant agent helping to prevent free radical damage to our brain cells throughout
our lifetime. The brain uses at least 10% of the body's oxygen at given moment, which it

requires to produce the energy brain cells need to for us to think and for the brain to process all
the conscious and unconscious information it responds to each moment of our lives. The brain is
a very metabolically active tissue that consumes much of the body's oxygen supply and hence,
generates an abundant amount of oxygen free radicals. Studies reveal that as much as 5% of the
oxygen consumed by our tissues create free radicals as a by-product of oxygen metabolism. As
the brain uses a great deal of the body's oxygen, it also generates a great deal of oxygen free
radicals in the process, and these free radicals are known to damage brain cells in such a way as
to contribute to the development of Alzheimer's disease, age-related decline in cognitive
function, and is associated with other neurodegenerative diseases (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's
disease, Lou Gehrig's disease, etc.)

One study shows that almost half of people over age 85 have Alzheimer's disease. In their quest
to understand which elderly individuals are most at risk for the development of memory loss
and/or Alzheimer's disease, Italian gerontologists discovered that older individuals with higher
melatonin levels had better mental acuity than those with low melatonin levels based upon a test
known as the Mini Mental State Exam. Japanese researchers have revealed the same finding in
that healthy functioning elderly subjects produce twice as much melatonin as Alzheimer's
disease patients of similar age, according to their investigative study. Researchers argue that
melatonin quenches oxygen free radicals produced in the brain sparing brain cells from their
damaging effects.

Free radicals have been shown to be a significant factor in brain cell damage characteristic of
Alzheimer's-type dementia, as evidenced by the fact that the brains of Alzheimer's patients
contain higher levels of amyloid protein, which is not only an end product of free radical attack,

but also generates additional free radicals within brain cells itself. Melatonin has been shown to
block the production of amyloid protein in animal studies, and is the antioxidant that most easily
gains entry into the brain. Many experts believe that the decline in melatonin secretion as we age
weakens the brain's antioxidant protection against oxygen free radicals, allowing them to more
easily damage brain cells, promoting memory loss, decline in cognitive function, the
development of Alzheimer's disease and contributes to the development or progression of other
neurodegenerative conditions. Melatonin also increases the synthesis of glutathione peroxidase,
which is another antioxidant (antioxidant enzyme) that has been shown to have a powerful effect
on preventing free radical damage in the brain.

A large intervention study in recent years (Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study),
demonstrated that high doses of Vitamin E (2,000 IU per day) could slow the progression of
moderately advanced Alzheimer's disease in human subjects. This effect was thought to be
mediated through the antioxidant function of Vitamin E. However, as mentioned earlier
melatonin more easily enters the brain than any other antioxidant nutrient and has also been
shown to quench free radicals in brain cells and boost brain levels of the antioxidant enzyme
glutathione peroxidase. As such, researchers have begun work to test whether melatonin
supplementation can prevent Alzheimer's-type conditions in animals.

Thus far, studies have revealed that melatonin can block important steps in the development of
Alzheimer's disease in animal testing. In a landmark study melatonin has recently been shown to
reverse the protein complex that is the hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, according to a published
report in the December 11, 2001 issue of the journal, Biochemistry , published by the American
Chemical Society.

The findings of the study were based upon experiments with animals and human brain cell
cultures. The researchers conclude, "Our results clearly demonstrate the ability of melatonin to
inhibit the process of forming the signature amyloid protein bundles seen in Alzheimer's
disease". In Alzheimer's disease, toxic fibrillar aggregates of a protein called amyloid beta
protein (amyloid protein) are the pathologic hallmark of the disease. In this study melatonin
inhibited the formation of amyloid protein, which is toxic to nerve cells and accelerates free
radical damage to neurons.

In this study, only melatonin protected brain cells from amyloid beta protein build up and
toxicity. Trials with Vitamin C, Vitamin E and a synthetic antioxidant were not protective in this
experimental study.

More research is required before any definitive statements can be made regarding the use of
melatonin and the prevention of Alzheimer's disease; however, it appears that the prevention of
excessive damage to our brain cells by oxygen free radicals may be another   important reason to
consider the use of melatonin supplementation, begin between age 40 and 50.

Melatonin Supplementation in Anti-Aging and Disease Prevention

Replacing the melatonin that the body no longer produces as we age may be an important aspect
of anti-aging and disease prevention. Melatonin is a very powerful antioxidant that quenches free
radicals in all body cells and tissues that are known to accelerate aging and increase our risk of
cancer. Melatonin supplementation has been shown to improve sleep quality and enhance
immune function, reversing certain aspects of the age-related decline in immune function.
Experimental and observational studies suggest that melatonin supplementation may help reduce
risk of breast and prostate cancer, and possibly other cancers. Melatonin is a powerful brain
antioxidant that protects the brain from free radicals linked to Alzheimer disease, age-related
cognitive decline and other degenerative conditions of the nervous system. Due to the significant
decline in melatonin secretion that occurs between age 40 and 50, many experts suggest taking a
melatonin supplement each day, beginning at this stage in life, to re-establish more youthful
levels of this important hormone and capitalize upon the many anti-aging and disease prevention
benefits it has been shown to provide.
Dosage Ranges of Melatonin
For anti-aging/disease prevention and/or sleep quality improving purposes, a nighttime dosage of
200 mcg (.2 mg) to 3,000 mcg (3 mg) is typically used. It is best to start with a small dose, in the
range of 200-300 mcg, and work up, based upon improved sleep with no awakening through the
night or morning drowsiness. Taking doses that are too high can result in morning grogginess,
headaches and/or abdominal cramps, and vivid dreams that may awaken you through the night.
Taking therapeutic doses of melatonin as an adjunct to the treatment of a disease or condition, in
the range of 5 – 75 mg per day, as is often used, should only be undertaken with knowledge of a
physician, who is able to monitor blood work and other parameters, as these dosages are still
experimental and long-term safety is unknown at this time
However, melatonin testing in humans and animals indicate that it is very non-toxic.

Contraindications and Drug-Nutrient Interactions
Some cases of depression can be aggravated by melatonin supplementation. Some antidepressant
drugs stimulate the production of melatonin and others, such as fluoxetine (Prozac), may lower
melatonin levels.  It is probably best at this time not to combine melatonin with any other drug
that targets brain chemistry or neurotransmitter levels (e.g. antidepressants, and drugs used to
manage bipolar disease, schizophrenia etc.
A number of drugs have been shown to deplete melatonin levels, which may induce a need to
begin replenishing melatonin at an earlier stage in life by those taking these drugs, which
include, aspirin, ibuprofen, beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers.

MELATONIN

James Meschino DC, MS, ROHP

Melatonin is a molecule that has been found in every animal and plant studied to date, from
human beings to the most primitive one-celled algae that evolved more than three billion years
ago.  In each organism, the molecular structure of melatonin is identical.  This sameness is a rare
occurrence in nature. In all the life forms studied, melatonin has been produced in the same
circadian (daily secretion pattern) rhythm, with higher levels produced at night than during the
daytime.
In humans, melatonin is produced and secreted by the pineal gland in the brain.  It is synthesized
from the brain chemical (neurotransmitter) serotonin, which itself is synthesized from 5-
hydroxytryptophan, which is originally derived from the amino acid tryptophan, found in many
foods. In the human body melatonin acts as a hormone, neurotransmitter (brain chemical),
antioxidant and immune system stimulator. This tremendous versatility accounts for the many
profound effects that melatonin exerts on our health status.
As a neurotransmitter (brain chemical) melatonin is best known for its ability to induce sleep in
persons with insomnia and to remedy problems with interrupted sleep, as well as its ability to
elevate mood.  Humans produce five to ten times more melatonin at night than during the day, a
circadian rhythm found in animals as well.  Peak amounts occur around two or three o'clock in
the morning. The darker the room, the more melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland at night.
After puberty the body's production of melatonin has been shown to decline.  By age 40 humans
often produce approximately 60 percent less melatonin than a 10 year old and by age 70 or 80
melatonin levels may be undetectable.  The use of certain drugs, such as aspirin, ibuprofen, and

--- Page Break ---

beta-blockers (used to control high blood pressure) also contributes to a decline in melatonin
levels.
With respect to its antioxidant properties, melatonin is unique in that it is both a water-soluble
antioxidant and a fat-soluble antioxidant.  This means that it can quench and intercept dangerous
free radicals in every area of the body and in every part of every cell in the body. Not even
vitamin C or vitamin E has this range of antioxidant capability. Some studies suggest that as an
antioxidant melatonin is twice as effective as Vitamin E, five times as efficient as glutathione,
and five hundred times more effective than the synthetic DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide).  However,
melatonin is produced in picograms (a trillionth of a gram – the smallest amount of any
hormone), whereas Vitamin E, and other antioxidants, are present in the body at much higher
concentrations.
The decline in melatonin synthesis and secretion by the pineal gland is considered to be a very
significant factor that contributes to less restful sleep, accelerated aging and increased risk of
certain cancers, dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and a weakening of our immune system as we
age. Many anti-aging experts recommend taking a melatonin supplement by age 50, as studies
suggest that providing more youthful levels of melatonin to your brain and body can help combat
aging, boost immune system function, reduce cancer and heart disease risk and produce better
quality sleep and mood enhancement.
Melatonin for a Good Night's Sleep
We sleep roughly 16 hours as infants, 8 hours in adolescence, 7 hours as adults, and less than 6
hours in our geriatric years.  No one seems to be exactly sure how melatonin induces better
quality, restful sleep, but the reduced output of melatonin as we age is strongly associated with
decreased sleep duration, a greater tendency towards interrupted sleep, and a lesser ability to
achieve deeper levels of sleep. Delta sleep, the deepest most restorative stage of sleep is longer in

--- Page Break ---

childhood, decreases at puberty, and progressively declines after age 30. The elderly spend less
time in this restorative stage and therefore, are likely to feel tired during the day. This accounts
for the fact that as we get older we often feel the need to rest more, but rarely feel completely
rested, rejuvenated, and completely re-energized after a night's sleep, as we did when we were
children.

Melatonin is made in the pineal gland from serotonin, which is a mood enhancing, appetite
suppressing, brain chemical (neurotransmitter). Daylight stimulates the production of serotonin
in our brain. That is one of the reason we feel so much better on a bright, sunny day, as the more
sunlight that enters the pupil of the eye, the greater is the synthesis of serotonin in our brain.
Darkness allows serotonin to be converted into melatonin in the pineal gland, and the darker the
room the more melatonin we secrete through the night. Starting in the evening, and through out
the night, the pineal gland releases melatonin, reaching peak levels between 2 and 4 am. In the
morning, exposure to light shuts off melatonin production.

An interesting study reported in the British Medical Journal in 1994 showed that the quality of
sleep in elderly individuals is proportional to the amount of melatonin secreted by their pineal
gland. Evidence suggests that cells within the pineal gland decrease in number as we age,
making them less efficient in producing melatonin, which in part, accounts for the decline in
melatonin secretions as we get older. Studies show that melatonin supplementation taken one
hour prior to bedtime helps individuals proceed more quickly into stage 2 sleep (early stage of
sleep) and remain longer in the deeper levels of sleep (stage 3, 4, and REM sleep-dream time
sleep) than occurs without melatonin supplementation.

--- Page Break ---

One of the ways that melatonin supplementation can strengthen our immune system is by helping
us attain deeper levels of sleep, as it is known that the immune system is most active during stage
3 and stage 4 sleep (delta sleep). However, many immune cells are also directly influenced by
melatonin, which has been shown to enhance many parameters of immune function.

Studies conducted on humans have shown that melatonin is an effective sleep aid, allowing older
subjects to experience the deeper, rejuvenating, immune-enhancing form of sleep we enjoyed in
our youth. As a sleep aid, melatonin has been shown to be safer than other sleeping pills, which
come with a host of side effects and toxicity problems. Melatonin toxicity studies demonstrate
that it is not only extremely non-toxic and safe, but it also provides many other health-
promoting, anti-aging benefits to the body beyond improving our sleep quality. Taken at the right
dosage, one hour before bedtime, melatonin does not produce morning drowsiness, and helps to
elevate mood and feeling of well being though out the day, which is probably due to its chemical
resemblance to serotonin – the mood elevating brain chemical. Anti-aging experts suggest that
we begin using melatonin supplementation between age 40 and 50, as a means to improve sleep
quality, support immune function, and to help reduce our risk of cancer, dementia, Alzheimer's
disease and possibly heart disease.
Melatonin May Prevent Breast and Prostate Cancer
The decline in melatonin secretion as we age may allow breast cancer and prostate cancer to
develop more easily, which may partially account for the increased incidence in these cancers as
we get older. Studies demonstrate that melatonin has an anti-estrogen effect on reproductive
tissues, which has been shown to tone down the over stimulation effect of estrogen on breast

--- Page Break ---

cells, an effect that is associated with decreased risk of breast cancer development. Some early
studies demonstrated that women who sleep in darker rooms throughout their lifetime, and who
therefore have higher secretion rates of melatonin through the night, have a lower risk of breast
cancer during their lifetime than do women who sleep in a room that is less dark.

More recently, experimental studies have shown that melatonin can reduce the replication rate of
human breast cancer cells by 50-75%, when these cells were exposed to alternating levels of
melatonin to mimic the body's day and night time melatonin secretion patterns. This was only
true in regards to breast cancer cells that possess estrogen receptors on their surface (estrogen-
receptor-positive breast cells), which indicates that melatonin likely latches on to estrogen
receptors, as does the hormone estrogen, but rather than stimulate these cells to divide rapidly, it
inhibits or slows their cell division rate. This is similar to the action of the drug Tamoxifen,
which is used to prevent the recurrence of breast cancer and its metastases, in women that have
estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer. In fact, experimental studies have shown that melatonin
can enhance the ability of Tamoxifen to inhibit the replication of breast cancer cells. These
studies prompted Dr. Paolo Lissoni to combine Tamoxifen therapy and melatonin
supplementation (20 mg twice per day) in a trial of breast cancer patients. The study showed that
four out of the fourteen women had a 50% or greater reduction in the size of their tumors. Eight
additional women showed no further progression in tumor size. Only two women failed to
respond to the treatment. These results were better than the typical outcomes associated with
Tamoxifen use alone. Larger studies of this kind are underway presently to better understand the
use of melatonin as a cancer therapy agent.

--- Page Break ---

However, from the standpoint of prevention, the body of evidence suggests that melatonin may
protect against breast cancer in several ways. First, it antagonizes the effects of estrogen on
breast cells, helping to slow down the rate of cell division, which in turn, decreases the chance of
a cancer cell developing. Second, should a cancer cell develop in the breast, melatonin has been
shown to inhibit its ability to divide and spread, giving the body's immune system a better
opportunity to kill it off before it can really take hold and become a life threatening problem.
Thirdly, melatonin enhances the effectiveness of the Natural Killer Cells, an important immune
cell that seeks out developing cancer cells and kills them before they can start to divide and
thrive in the body. Also keep in mind that melatonin is a powerful antioxidant that helps to
prevent free radical damage (and the genetic mutations they cause) to all body tissues and all
cellular components, including the DNA of breast cells. Thus, the lower melatonin levels that are
found in a woman's body after 50 years of age (men and women 51-55 years of age secrete half
as much melatonin at night as is secreted at age 21-25; melatonin secretion is four times lower in
men and women 82-86 years of age than at age 21-25) may reduce a woman's ability to prevent
the development and spread of breast cancer. Thus, many anti-aging experts recommend that
women take 200 mcg (.2 mg) -3,000 mcg (3 mg) of melatonin an hour before bedtime each
night, beginning at age 40-50, to re-acquire the protective levels of melatonin that may help
guard against breast cancer in younger women.

In regards to prostate cancer, studies by R. Philo and A. Berkowitz, published in the Journal of
Urology in 1988, showed that melatonin inhibits the growth and replication of human prostate
cancer cells. More recently, an experimental study by David Blask and another group of
researchers demonstrated similar findings, showing a 50% reduction in prostate cancer cell
growth and replication when these cells were incubated with melatonin. Like breast cancer

patients, males with diagnosed prostate cancer have been shown to have low blood levels of

There is one important case study that showed that melatonin supplementation at 6 mg per day
was able to reduce the PSA level from 30 to 4 within six months in a confirmed case of localized

melatonin one hour before bedtime each night. This intervention may help reverse or better
control prostate cancer cell activity, which may help improve outcomes from concurrent or
future medical interventions (drugs, surgery, radiation treatment).

However, in regards to prevention, the body of evidence suggests that melatonin
supplementation by age 40-50 years of age, may be another intervention that can help deter
development of prostate cancer, which remains the most frequently diagnosed cancer in men in
North America.

Melatonin Boosts Immune Function

Many studies have shown that melatonin can boost various aspects of immune function and thus,
the decline in melatonin levels as we age may be an significant contributing factor to the parallel
decline in immune function that occurs after age 40 to 50. Receptors for melatonin have been
found in lymphoid organs such as the thymus gland and spleen, and on certain white blood cells.
Some studies suggest that melatonin can help restore thymus gland function and prevent age-
related thymus gland degeneration. Studies on mice demonstrate that melatonin can enhance
immune function even when mice were given cortisol, a drug known to suppress the immune
system. Melatonin supplementation also showed that it could keep the immune system working
at a more optimal level in mice that were subjected to various types of stress. Stress is also
known to suppress immune function, but melatonin administration buffered the immune system
against the effects of stress to a significant degree in these studies.

--- Page Break ---

The work of researchers G.J. Maestroni and A. Contri, and fellow investigators, has provided us
with an important piece of the puzzle as to how melatonin helps to optimize the function of our
immune system. They have shown that the T-Helper Cells of our immune system have receptors
for melatonin. When melatonin attaches to these receptors a cascade of events is set into motion
that significantly boosts our immune function. Once melatonin docks to the receptors on our T-
Helper Cells, they in turn stimulate the release of an important immune system signaling agent
known as interleukin-4 (IL-4), which increases the production and efficiency of Natural Killer
Cells, and stimulates immune cells to more efficiently engulf and destroy various micro-
organisms (viruses, bacteria, yeast fungi etc.). Studies show that taking 2 mg of melatonin at
night can increase the production of Natural Killer Cells by 240% compared to pre-melatonin
supplementation levels. Natural Killer Cells specialize in attacking cancer cells and virus-
infected cells, two extremely important aspects in the prevention of cancer and the infections
disease process, served by our immune system. The release of IL-4 also stimulates the
production of a hormone-like substance (granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor) that
increases the production of white blood cells in our bone marrow. White blood cells are the cells
of the immune system that battle infections and cancer cells in our bloodstream and in all the
tissues and organs of the body.

The importance of T-Helper Cells in coordinating the movements, proliferation and efficiency of
our immune cells (white blood cells) is highlighted by the fact that the primary way in which the
HIV-virus exerts its lethal effects is by infecting our T-Helper cells, suppressing their function
and decreasing their numbers in the body. When T-Helper Cell concentrations fall below a
critical threshold (200 cells per microliter) due to infection with the HIV-virus, this is the point
where AIDS begins, whereby opportunistic infections, general deterioration and increased

--- Page Break ---

susceptibility to malignancy become more prevalent in these cases. In fact, studies by G.
Maestoni and fellow researchers have shown that melatonin supplementation of 20 mg per day
(taken at 7:00 PM), given to fourteen patients with HIV infection or full blown AIDS was able to
raise the T-Helper Cell blood count by 35%, on average. It also raised the concentrations of
Natural Killer Cells by 57%, and raised the levels of one type of lymphocyte by 76%. None of
the patients had any adverse side effects from melatonin supplementation at this dosage. Other
studies by Dr. Maestoni as well as Dr. Lissoni, have shown that the melatonin supplementation
can produce a number of favorable outcomes on the immune system in HIV and AIDS patients,
when administered in conjunction with other standard HIV drugs. These studies provide
definitive evidence that melatonin enhances important aspects of immune function, even in
individuals with compromised immune diseases.

There is reason to believe that daily melatonin supplementation after age 40-50, when our body's
secretion rates of this hormone have reached a critical point of decline, may be highly
advantageous in preventing the deterioration in immune function that commonly accompanies
the normal aging process and makes us more prone to cancer and life-threatening infectious
diseases.
Melatonin May Reduce Risk of Alzheimer's Disease and Age-Related Cognitive
Impairment

Melatonin is not only made by a gland in the brain (pineal gland), but may be the brain's most
powerful antioxidant agent helping to prevent free radical damage to our brain cells throughout
our lifetime. The brain uses at least 10% of the body's oxygen at given moment, which it

--- Page Break ---

requires to produce the energy brain cells need to for us to think and for the brain to process all
the conscious and unconscious information it responds to each moment of our lives. The brain is
a very metabolically active tissue that consumes much of the body's oxygen supply and hence,
generates an abundant amount of oxygen free radicals. Studies reveal that as much as 5% of the
oxygen consumed by our tissues create free radicals as a by-product of oxygen metabolism. As
the brain uses a great deal of the body's oxygen, it also generates a great deal of oxygen free
radicals in the process, and these free radicals are known to damage brain cells in such a way as
to contribute to the development of Alzheimer's disease, age-related decline in cognitive
function, and is associated with other neurodegenerative diseases (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's
disease, Lou Gehrig's disease, etc.)

One study shows that almost half of people over age 85 have Alzheimer's disease. In their quest
to understand which elderly individuals are most at risk for the development of memory loss
and/or Alzheimer's disease, Italian gerontologists discovered that older individuals with higher
melatonin levels had better mental acuity than those with low melatonin levels based upon a test
known as the Mini Mental State Exam. Japanese researchers have revealed the same finding in
that healthy functioning elderly subjects produce twice as much melatonin as Alzheimer's
disease patients of similar age, according to their investigative study. Researchers argue that
melatonin quenches oxygen free radicals produced in the brain sparing brain cells from their
damaging effects.

Free radicals have been shown to be a significant factor in brain cell damage characteristic of
Alzheimer's-type dementia, as evidenced by the fact that the brains of Alzheimer's patients
contain higher levels of amyloid protein, which is not only an end product of free radical attack,

--- Page Break ---

but also generates additional free radicals within brain cells itself. Melatonin has been shown to
block the production of amyloid protein in animal studies, and is the antioxidant that most easily
gains entry into the brain. Many experts believe that the decline in melatonin secretion as we age
weakens the brain's antioxidant protection against oxygen free radicals, allowing them to more
easily damage brain cells, promoting memory loss, decline in cognitive function, the
development of Alzheimer's disease and contributes to the development or progression of other
neurodegenerative conditions. Melatonin also increases the synthesis of glutathione peroxidase,
which is another antioxidant (antioxidant enzyme) that has been shown to have a powerful effect
on preventing free radical damage in the brain.

A large intervention study in recent years (Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study),
demonstrated that high doses of Vitamin E (2,000 IU per day) could slow the progression of
moderately advanced Alzheimer's disease in human subjects. This effect was thought to be
mediated through the antioxidant function of Vitamin E. However, as mentioned earlier
melatonin more easily enters the brain than any other antioxidant nutrient and has also been
shown to quench free radicals in brain cells and boost brain levels of the antioxidant enzyme
glutathione peroxidase. As such, researchers have begun work to test whether melatonin
supplementation can prevent Alzheimer's-type conditions in animals.

Thus far, studies have revealed that melatonin can block important steps in the development of
Alzheimer's disease in animal testing. In a landmark study melatonin has recently been shown to
reverse the protein complex that is the hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, according to a published
report in the December 11, 2001 issue of the journal, Biochemistry , published by the American
Chemical Society.

--- Page Break ---

The findings of the study were based upon experiments with animals and human brain cell
cultures. The researchers conclude, "Our results clearly demonstrate the ability of melatonin to
inhibit the process of forming the signature amyloid protein bundles seen in Alzheimer's
disease". In Alzheimer's disease, toxic fibrillar aggregates of a protein called amyloid beta
protein (amyloid protein) are the pathologic hallmark of the disease. In this study melatonin
inhibited the formation of amyloid protein, which is toxic to nerve cells and accelerates free
radical damage to neurons.

In this study, only melatonin protected brain cells from amyloid beta protein build up and
toxicity. Trials with Vitamin C, Vitamin E and a synthetic antioxidant were not protective in this
experimental study.

More research is required before any definitive statements can be made regarding the use of
melatonin and the prevention of Alzheimer's disease; however, it appears that the prevention of
excessive damage to our brain cells by oxygen free radicals may be another   important reason to
consider the use of melatonin supplementation, begin between age 40 and 50.

Melatonin Supplementation in Anti-Aging and Disease Prevention

--- Page Break ---

Replacing the melatonin that the body no longer produces as we age may be an important aspect
of anti-aging and disease prevention. Melatonin is a very powerful antioxidant that quenches free
radicals in all body cells and tissues that are known to accelerate aging and increase our risk of
cancer. Melatonin supplementation has been shown to improve sleep quality and enhance
immune function, reversing certain aspects of the age-related decline in immune function.
Experimental and observational studies suggest that melatonin supplementation may help reduce
risk of breast and prostate cancer, and possibly other cancers. Melatonin is a powerful brain
antioxidant that protects the brain from free radicals linked to Alzheimer disease, age-related
cognitive decline and other degenerative conditions of the nervous system. Due to the significant
decline in melatonin secretion that occurs between age 40 and 50, many experts suggest taking a
melatonin supplement each day, beginning at this stage in life, to re-establish more youthful
levels of this important hormone and capitalize upon the many anti-aging and disease prevention
benefits it has been shown to provide.
Dosage Ranges of Melatonin
For anti-aging/disease prevention and/or sleep quality improving purposes, a nighttime dosage of
200 mcg (.2 mg) to 3,000 mcg (3 mg) is typically used. It is best to start with a small dose, in the
range of 200-300 mcg, and work up, based upon improved sleep with no awakening through the
night or morning drowsiness. Taking doses that are too high can result in morning grogginess,
headaches and/or abdominal cramps, and vivid dreams that may awaken you through the night.
Taking therapeutic doses of melatonin as an adjunct to the treatment of a disease or condition, in
the range of 5 – 75 mg per day, as is often used, should only be undertaken with knowledge of a
physician, who is able to monitor blood work and other parameters, as these dosages are still
experimental and long-term safety is unknown at this time
However, melatonin testing in humans and animals indicate that it is very non-toxic.

--- Page Break ---

Contraindications and Drug-Nutrient Interactions
Some cases of depression can be aggravated by melatonin supplementation. Some antidepressant
drugs stimulate the production of melatonin and others, such as fluoxetine (Prozac), may lower
melatonin levels.  It is probably best at this time not to combine melatonin with any other drug
that targets brain chemistry or neurotransmitter levels (e.g. antidepressants, and drugs used to
manage bipolar disease, schizophrenia etc.
A number of drugs have been shown to deplete melatonin levels, which may induce a need to
begin replenishing melatonin at an earlier stage in life by those taking these drugs, which
include, aspirin, ibuprofen, beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers.
